newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Key Lithuanian rural voters bitter as poll nears.
newsitem.headline: Key Lithuanian rural voters bitter as poll nears.

text.p: Lithuanian politicians are trying hard to woo the votes of the country's farmers ahead of weekend elections but the mood of this key electorate is bitter, farmers and analysts said on Thursday.

Five years after Lithuania quit the former Soviet Union and embraced the market economy, life in this village has hardly changed as a woman washed her clothes in a brook by a pot-holed lane while farmers rode past in horse-drawn wagons.
This is in stark contrast to the capital Vilnius, 30 kms (18 miles) north, where many bars, restaurants and the other trappings of the West have sprung up.
"The politicians have improved their own lives but they have not done anything for us," said one 72-year-old farmer, who refused to be named, sitting in his wagon.
He, like many farmers, said he was forced to eke out a living on tiny plots of land with outdated equipment.
Around one third of the 3.6 million population lives in the countryside and their choice in the elections, which take place in two rounds on October 20 and November 10, will be key.

The right-wing Homeland Union party, headed by Vytautas Landsbergis, who spearheaded Lithuania's independence drive, is hoping to displace the former Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
In 1992, they were one of the main reasons that Lithuania propelled former Communists back into power, starting a trend later mirrored in other eastern European states.
The rural population was then reeling from the crash decollectivisation by Landsbergis' party, then named Sajudis, and orchestrated by former prime minister Gediminas Vagnorius.
They overwhelmingly backed the former Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP) and a year later helped its leader, Algirdas Brazauskas, to become president.
But four years on, many farmers fail to see how the LDLP has helped them, despite their promises to ease their pain.
Analysts said it was not clear which way farmers would vote but that the Farmers Party and the Christian Democrats may pick up their support.
"When the kolkhozes (collective farms) were operating, life was better here," the farmer said.
"There were more things available to farmers, such as oil, gas and machinery. There are enough goods in the shops today but no one has the money to buy them," he added.
He also complained of a minuscule pension of 180 litas ($45) a month.
The 1995 United Nations Human Development (UNDP) report for Lithuania said that rural incomes at the end of 1995 were just 29 percent of their 1990 levels.
It said more than 20 percent of the population worked in agriculture although the sector accounts for just seven percent of the economy, down from 11 percent in 1993.
Income distribution has also widened, with gross per capita income for urban dwellers at 280 litas ($70) in 1995, 43 percent higher than the 195 litas ($49) brought home by rural residents.
"The disintergration of the collectives hit rural residents very painfully and there are few opportunities in the countryside," said UNDP researcher Irene Voloschuk.
The farmer said that like many people in Lithuania he had not decided who to vote for.
"What can the state do for us?" he said with a shrug of this shoulders. "Lithuania is poor".
